daily.description: Explaining your daily pet care.
daily.example: Making breakfast for the cat is my job every morning.

work.title: Mentoring a junior
work.description: Telling a coworker how you helped a new hire.
work.example: I showed the new hire how to do the job.

work.title: Avoid with superiors
work.description: Don't say 「〜てあげましょうか」 to a superior. Use the humble 「お〜します」 instead.
work.example: Shall I carry the documents for you, sir? (not ✕持ってあげましょうか)

etymology: あげる is written 「上げる」, originally meaning "to raise, to lift up". Lifting something up to offer it to a person of higher status gave rise to the meaning "to give". It was originally a humble word but gradually became neutral, meaning ordinary "give", so its original humble role was taken over by さしあげる (差し上げる).
formation: 「〜てあげる」 = verb te-form + 「あげる」 (「上げる」: to give; originally “to raise, to offer up”). The main verb 「あげる」 means “give something to someone”; after the te-form, the “thing” is replaced by an “action”: you give the act of doing something to the other person like a gift → do something for someone. Because the direction is “me → them”, the beneficiary can't be the speaker; and because it literally means “bestowing a favor”, saying it to a superior's face sounds like “I'm doing you a favor”, which is rude.

similar.title: 〜てさしあげる
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「さしあげる」 is the humble form of 「あげる」, used for doing things for superiors (「先生のかばんを持ってさしあげた」); but it still shouldn't be said to their face — it's mostly used when telling a third party.

similar.title: 〜てやる
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「やる」 is “give” to juniors, animals, or plants; 「〜てやる」 is used for doing things for children or pets (「犬を散歩させてやる」) and can also express determination or a threat, with a rough tone.

similar.title: 〜てくれる
similar.explanation: Both are giving-and-receiving auxiliaries. 「〜てあげる」 is me doing something for others; 「〜てくれる」 is others doing something for me — the opposite direction, with the speaker's side as the beneficiary.

similar.title: 〜てもらう
similar.explanation: Both are giving-and-receiving auxiliaries. 「〜てもらう」 takes the receiver as the subject (「友だちに手伝ってもらう」); 「〜てあげる」 takes the giver as the subject (「友だちを手伝ってあげる」).

meaning: Someone does something for the speaker (or their side), and the speaker is grateful. Use 「てくださる」 for superiors.
connection: Verb te-form + くれる (honorific: 〜てくださる)

senses.label: Someone does it for me
senses.meaning: The giver is the subject, and the receiver is “me” or my side. 「私に」 is usually left out. It conveys gratitude.
senses.connection: Person が + verb te-form + くれる／くれた
examples: My friends helped me move.
Thank you for coming.
My mom always listens to me.

senses.label: A superior does it for me
senses.meaning: 「〜てくださる」 is the honorific form, for when an elder or superior does something for you. Its masu-form is 「くださいます」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + くださる／くださいます／くださった
examples: My teacher corrected my essay for me.
The company president drove me to the station.

senses.label: Requests
senses.meaning: 「〜てくれない？」 and 「〜てくれませんか」 ask someone for help, more softly than 「〜てください」. 「〜てくれ」 is a blunt order used by men toward equals or juniors.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + くれない？／くれませんか／くれ
examples: Could you pass me the salt?
Excuse me, could you open the door for me?

notes: Only used when someone does something for “me or my side”; between outsiders, use 「〜てあげる」: ✕「田中さんが山田さんに教えてくれた」→ ○「教えてあげた」.
Don't use 「くれる」 for bosses or elders: ✕「部長が教えてくれました」→ ○「教えてくださいました」; when asking, ✕「〜てくれない？」→ ○「〜ていただけませんか」.
When someone helps you, 「〜てくれた」 is what expresses your gratitude; just saying 「先輩が手伝いました」 sounds cold, as if you didn't appreciate it.
「〜てくれ」 is a masculine command and very rough when said to others.

daily.title: Thanking a friend
daily.description: Thanking a friend for making the effort to visit.
daily.example: Thanks for coming all this way.

daily.title: Asking family for help at the table
daily.description: Casually asking someone to pass something.
daily.example: Can you pass the soy sauce?

daily.title: Talking about family help
daily.description: Telling a friend about a parent's support.
daily.example: My dad gave me a ride to the station.

work.title: Thanking your boss
work.description: Showing gratitude for guidance with the honorific form.
work.example: The department manager took the time to teach me carefully.

work.title: Asking a coworker for help
work.description: A small favor asked in a soft tone.
work.example: Could you make a copy of this for me?

etymology: くれる is written 「呉れる」; the old verb 「くる（呉る）」 meant "to give (to an inferior, to oneself)". From the medieval period on it was used specifically in the direction "someone gives to me", forming, together with あげる and もらう, Japanese's distinctive system of giving and receiving verbs. くださる is written 「下さる」, originally "to bestow (from above)", hence its honorific nature.
formation: 「〜てくれる」 = verb te-form + 「くれる」 (「呉れる」: someone gives to me). The main verb 「くれる」 specifically means “someone gives something to the speaker's side”; after the te-form, the “thing” becomes an “action” → someone does something for me. Because 「くれる」 always points toward the speaker, it shows that we are the beneficiaries even without 「私に」; and since it treats the other person as the giver of a favor, it naturally carries gratitude. For superiors it changes to the honorific 「くださる」.

similar.title: 〜てくださる
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「くださる」 is the honorific form of 「くれる」, used when superiors or bosses do something for me (「先生が直してくださった」).

similar.title: 〜てもらう
similar.explanation: Two ways of saying the same thing: 「友だちが手伝ってくれた」 takes the giver as the subject and stresses their kindness; 「友だちに手伝ってもらった」 takes me as the subject and can imply “I asked them to”.

similar.title: 〜てもらえませんか・〜てくれませんか
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「〜てくれませんか」 and 「〜てもらえませんか」 are both polite requests; the latter takes yourself as the subject and sounds a little more polite.

meaning: You have someone do something for you, or you benefit from someone's action. Use 「ていただく」 for superiors.
connection: Verb te-form + もらう (humble: 〜ていただく)

senses.label: Having someone do it for me
senses.meaning: The receiver (usually me) is the subject, and the giver is marked with 「に」. It can mean you asked for it or simply that you benefited: “have / get someone to ...”.
senses.connection: Person に + verb te-form + もらう; for superiors: 〜ていただく
examples: I had my friends help me move.
I had a doctor examine me at the hospital.
My teacher kindly corrected my essay.

senses.label: Polite requests
senses.meaning: 「〜てもらえませんか」 and 「〜ていただけませんか」 are very polite, very common request forms: “Could you possibly ...?”.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + もらえませんか／いただけませんか
examples: Excuse me, could you take a picture for me?
Could you explain it once more, please?

senses.label: Wanting someone to do
senses.meaning: 「〜てもらいたい」 and 「〜ていただきたい」 express wanting someone to do something. More formal than 「〜てほしい」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + もらいたい／いただきたい
examples: I'd really like you to read this book.
We'd like all of you to take part as well.

notes: The giver takes 「に」; get the particle wrong and the meaning changes: ✕「友だちが手伝ってもらった」 (= my friend got help from someone) → ○「友だちに手伝ってもらった」.
With bosses and clients, use 「〜ていただく」; when asking, 「〜てもらえませんか」 still isn't formal enough for clients — say 「〜ていただけますでしょうか」.
Saying 「〜てもらいたいです」 directly to a superior sounds demanding; put it softly as 「〜ていただけるとありがたいです」.
「〜てもらった」 can imply “I asked them to”; when someone helped on their own initiative, 「〜てくれた」 better shows their kindness.

daily.title: Asking someone to take a photo
daily.description: Politely asking a passerby at a tourist spot.
daily.example: Excuse me, could you press the shutter for me?

daily.title: Talking about a friend's help
daily.description: Telling family how a friend helped.
daily.example: A friend gave me a ride to the station.

daily.title: At the hair salon
daily.description: Saying you got your hair cut.
daily.example: I got my hair cut yesterday.

work.title: Asking your boss to review something
work.description: Politely asking a superior to check materials.
work.example: Could you take a look at these materials?

work.title: Assigning a task to a junior
work.description: Saying what you want them to do.
work.example: I'd like you to have this summarized by tomorrow.

etymology: もらう is written 「貰う」, originally meaning "to ask for and receive". いただく is written 「頂く／戴く」, originally "to place on top of one's head" — when receiving something from a person of higher status, one raised it above one's head out of respect — and so it became the humble word for "to receive" (the 「いただきます」 said before meals comes from this too).
formation: 「〜てもらう」 = verb te-form + 「もらう」 (「貰う」: to receive, to get). The main verb 「もらう」 means “I get something from someone”; after the te-form, the “thing” becomes an “action” → “receive” an action from someone. Since the subject is the receiver, the giver is marked as the source with 「に／から」; and since what you “get” is often something you asked for, it often implies “I asked them to”, which is why the potential 「〜てもらえませんか」 becomes a polite request.

similar.title: 〜ていただく
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「いただく」 is the humble form of 「もらう」, used for receiving help from superiors or bosses (「先生に教えていただいた」).

similar.title: 〜てくれる
similar.explanation: Same event: 「〜てくれる」 takes the giver as the subject and stresses that they acted for me of their own accord; 「〜てもらう」 takes me as the subject and can imply “I asked”.

similar.title: 〜てほしい・〜てもらいたい
similar.explanation: Same origin and similar meaning. 「〜てもらいたい」 is simply this pattern + 「たい」; like 「〜てほしい」, it means “want someone to do ...”. 「〜てほしい」 is more direct and casual.

similar.title: 〜てもらえませんか・〜てくれませんか
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「〜てもらえませんか」 is the negative-question potential form of this pattern, used specifically for polite requests; with superiors, use 「〜ていただけませんか」.

meaning: Lists parallel facts or reasons (“... and ..., and ...”), or gives one or two reasons while implying there are more.
connection: Plain form + し (noun / na-adjective: 〜だし); also after polite forms: 〜ですし／〜ますし

senses.label: Listing
senses.meaning: Lists several facts or features pointing the same way (all good or all bad): “not only ... but also ...”. Often paired with 「も」.
senses.connection: Aし、Bし、(それに) C; often 「〜も〜し、〜も〜」
examples: This apartment is spacious and close to the station, so it's really convenient.
He's kind, and he's a good cook too.
He's smart, and he has a great personality.

senses.label: Giving reasons
senses.meaning: Gives one or two reasons, implies there are others, then leads to a conclusion. It sounds softer than 「から」 and doesn't pin everything on one reason.
senses.connection: Reason + し、(reason + し、) + conclusion
examples: It's raining and it's cold today, so I don't want to go out.
We're short on time, so let's take a taxi.

senses.label: Sentence-final excuse
senses.meaning: At the end of a sentence, it states only the reason and leaves the conclusion for the listener to infer, like “... you know”. Often used in speech to make excuses softly.
senses.connection: Plain form + し。(often with 「だって」)
examples: Well, it's raining.
It's fine. I'm free anyway.

notes: Ending a sentence with 「〜し。」 sounds like making excuses or talking back (「だって、暇だし」); using it with bosses or clients sounds defiant and impolite.
Nouns and na-adjectives take 「だ」: ✕「雨し」→ ○「雨だし」; ✕「静かし」→ ○「静かだし」.
Turning down an invitation with a single 「〜し」 reason (「忙しいし…」) sounds like an excuse; to decline formally, say 「申し訳ありませんが、〜ので」.

daily.title: Recommending a restaurant
daily.description: Listing a place's good points for a friend.
daily.example: That place is cheap and tasty. I recommend it.

daily.title: Turning down an invitation
daily.description: Listing reasons to decline gently.
daily.example: I'm tired today, and I have an early start tomorrow, so I'm heading home.

daily.title: A sentence-final excuse
daily.description: Giving a reason when asked why you didn't do something.
daily.example: Well, it's such a hassle.

work.title: Making a suggestion in a meeting
work.description: Listing reasons to support a proposal, using polite 「ですし」.
work.example: It's cheap and it doesn't take much time, so I think this method is best.

work.title: Evaluating a new hire
work.description: Listing a new employee's strengths to your boss.
work.example: He works fast, and he's conscientious.

etymology: The conjunctive particle 「し」 is generally thought to derive from 「し」, the attributive form of the Classical Japanese past auxiliary 「き」, or from the emphatic adverbial particle 「し」; from the early modern period it developed into a conjunctive particle for listing parallel items and reasons. There are several theories about its origin, and none is settled.
formation: 「〜し」 is a conjunctive particle that attaches after a complete plain-form sentence (with tense and 「だ」), “laying out” that fact as one item before going on to the next. Since what comes before is a complete sentence, noun sentences keep 「だ」 (「雨だし」). Laying out one item implies “there's more”, so even with just one reason it hints at “and not only that”; these listed facts are used to support a conclusion, which makes it “listing reasons”.

similar.title: 〜から (cause / reason)
similar.explanation: 「〜から」 clearly states one cause; 「〜し」 lists several reasons, or gives one while implying there are others, with a softer tone.

similar.title: 〜上に
similar.explanation: 「〜上に」 (N3) also means “not only ... but also”, stacking facts in the same direction, and is more written (「この店は安い上においしい」); 「〜し」 is more conversational and is often used to list reasons.

similar.title: 〜たり〜たりする
similar.explanation: 「〜たり〜たり」 lists actions (as examples); 「〜し」 lists facts, qualities, and reasons.

meaning: Something goes beyond the proper limit: “too ...”, “over-...”. Usually negative.
connection: Verb masu-stem + すぎる; i-adjective minus い + すぎる (いい→よすぎる, ない→なさすぎる); na-adjective stem + すぎる

senses.label: Doing too much
senses.meaning: With verbs, it means overdoing an action: “too much”, “over-...”.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem + すぎる (食べすぎる, 飲みすぎる, 働きすぎる)
examples: I ate too much cake yesterday.
Please don't drink too much.

senses.label: Too ...
senses.meaning: With adjectives, a quality goes beyond what is appropriate: “too ...”, “overly ...”.
senses.connection: i-adjective minus い / na-adjective stem + すぎる
examples: This bag is too expensive for me to buy.
This room is too quiet. It feels a bit lonely.
Having too little confidence isn't good either.

senses.label: Noun 「〜すぎ」
senses.meaning: As the noun 「〜すぎ」, it refers to the excess itself. Very common in speech.
senses.connection: Verb masu-stem / adjective stem + すぎ(だ／に)
examples: That's going a bit too far.
Be careful not to overeat.

notes: For i-adjectives, drop the 「い」 first: ✕「高いすぎる」→ ○「高すぎる」; 「いい」→「よすぎる」, 「ない」→「なさすぎる」.
Commenting directly on someone's looks or behavior (「太りすぎですよ」, 「派手すぎる」) is very rude; Japanese people generally don't say such things to someone's face.

「すぎる」 carries a negative judgment, so be careful using it as praise: 「親切すぎる」 can mean “overly helpful, meddling”. Exaggerated compliments like 「かわいすぎる」 in casual speech are only for people you're close to.

daily.title: After a big meal
daily.description: Feeling uncomfortable from eating too much.
daily.example: I'm stuffed. I ate too much.

daily.title: Shopping
daily.description: Deciding something is too pricey to buy.
daily.example: This coat is a bit too expensive.

daily.title: Over-the-top praise
daily.description: Reacting to a cute little animal.
daily.example: This kitten is way too cute!

work.title: Worrying about an overworked coworker
work.description: Telling a coworker not to wear themselves out.
work.example: Haven't you been working too hard lately? Take a little break.

work.title: Evaluating a plan
work.description: Pointing out a problem with the plan.
work.example: I think this schedule is too tight.

etymology: すぎる is written with the kanji meaning "pass", and originally meant "to pass by, to go through (a place or time)". Going past a certain point means "exceeding" it, which extended to "going beyond the limit" in degree. In Classical Japanese it was the kami-nidan verb すぐ, which later became the kami-ichidan すぎる. (English "overdo" and "go too far" follow a similar logic.)
formation: 「〜すぎる」 = verb masu-stem / adjective stem + 「すぎる」 (「過ぎる」: to pass, to go beyond). The main verb 「過ぎる」 means “go past a point” (「駅を過ぎる」); after an action or quality, it means “the degree has gone past the appropriate line” → excess. Going past the line means exceeding what's acceptable, so it usually carries a negative judgment. It attaches to tenseless stems and forms a new ichidan verb, which can become 「すぎた」 or 「すぎて」; the masu-stem 「すぎ」 can also be used as a noun (「飲みすぎ」).

similar.title: 〜あまり（に）
similar.explanation: 「あまり（に）」 (N3), as an adverb, also means “too” (「あまりに高い」) and is often used together with 「すぎる」; 「〜すぎる」 attaches after words and is used more widely.

similar.title: 〜にすぎない
similar.explanation: Same origin, both from 「過ぎる」. 「〜にすぎない」 (N2) means “nothing more than ...”, showing a low degree not worth mentioning (「冗談にすぎない」); it's different from the “excess” 「すぎる」, so keep them apart.

meaning: Something is easy or convenient to do, or something tends to happen: “easy to ...”, “prone to ...”.
connection: Verb masu-stem + やすい

senses.label: Easy to do
senses.meaning: An action is easy or convenient to do. Usually positive: “easy to ...”.
senses.connection: Volitional verb masu-stem + やすい (読みやすい, 使いやすい, わかりやすい)
examples: This pen is really easy to write with.
The teacher's explanation was easy to understand.
I want a computer that's easy to use.

senses.label: Prone to happen
senses.meaning: Something tends to change or happen easily. Usually with non-volitional verbs, and often negative: “prone to ...”, “tends to ...”.
senses.connection: Non-volitional verb masu-stem + やすい (割れやすい, 風邪をひきやすい)
examples: It's easy to catch a cold in winter, so please take care.
This glass breaks easily.

notes: Only attaches to the verb masu-stem: ✕「食べるやすい」→ ○「食べやすい」; nouns and adjectives can't attach directly.
Calling someone 「わかりやすい人」 can be taken as “wears their heart on their sleeve, simple”, so mind the context when saying it to their face.
The “likely to happen” use is mostly for unwanted things (「割れやすい」, 「忘れやすい」); to say what someone often does, written language often uses 「〜がちだ」.

daily.title: Choosing a product
daily.description: Comparing items in a shop.
daily.example: This bag is light and easy to carry.

daily.title: Talking about health
daily.description: Saying you get sick easily when seasons change.
daily.example: It's easy to get run down when the seasons change.

daily.title: Recommending a study book
daily.description: Telling a friend about an easy-to-follow book.
daily.example: This book is really easy to understand.

work.title: Improving materials
work.description: A boss asks for clearer documents.
work.example: Please make the materials a little easier to read.

work.title: Describing the workplace
work.description: Telling a coworker about the new office.
work.example: The new office is spacious and easy to work in.

etymology: やすい is written 「易い」 and shares its origin with 「安い」; the old word 「やすし」 originally meant "calm, carefree, at ease". From "feeling at ease" it extended to "easy to do", and it became the second element of compound adjectives after the verb continuative form.
formation: 「〜やすい」 = verb masu-stem + 「やすい」 (「易い」: easy, effortless), generally thought to share a root with 「安い」, originally meaning “light, no trouble”. Together they form a new i-adjective meaning “this action takes no effort”. With an intentional action by a person (「読む」, 「使う」) → easy to do; with a non-volitional change (「割れる」, 「忘れる」) → likely to happen. Since the whole thing is an i-adjective, it conjugates like one (「やすかった」, 「やすくない」).

similar.title: 〜がち
similar.explanation: 「〜がち」 (N2) means “tend to, often (something bad happens)”, stressing frequency and tendency (「病気がちだ」 = often sick); 「〜やすい」 stresses the quality of being prone to something (「病気になりやすい」 = gets sick easily).

similar.title: 〜っぽい
similar.explanation: 「〜っぽい」 (N3) after a verb masu-stem also means “tending to ...” (「忘れっぽい」, 「怒りっぽい」), but only describes personality and is casual; 「〜やすい」 can describe both people and things.

similar.title: 〜かねない
similar.explanation: 「〜かねない」 (N2) means “could lead to (a bad result)” (「事故になりかねない」), a warning about danger; 「〜やすい」 only says something is likely by nature, and it isn't necessarily bad.

meaning: Something is hard or awkward to do, or doesn't easily happen: “hard to ...”, “not easily ...”.
connection: Verb masu-stem + にくい

senses.label: Hard to do
senses.meaning: An action is difficult or inconvenient to do: “hard to ...”.
senses.connection: Volitional verb masu-stem + にくい (読みにくい, 歩きにくい, 使いにくい)
examples: This writing is so small it's hard to read.
My new shoes were still hard to walk in.

senses.label: Awkward to say or ask
senses.meaning: Hesitating to do something out of consideration for others: “it's awkward to ...”, “hard to bring up”.
senses.connection: Masu-stem of 「言う」, 「聞く」, 「頼む」, etc. + にくい
examples: There are some things I feel awkward asking my teacher.
He looks busy, so it's hard to ask him.

senses.label: Doesn't easily happen
senses.meaning: Something doesn't change or happen easily. Here it's usually positive and often describes product features.
senses.connection: Non-volitional verb masu-stem + にくい (割れにくい, 燃えにくい, 汚れにくい)
examples: This glass doesn't break easily.
These clothes are made of a stain-resistant material.

notes: Only attaches to the verb masu-stem: ✕「読むにくい」→ ○「読みにくい」.
「言いにくいんですが…」 is the set lead-in Japanese people use before bad news or a request; when you hear it, expect something awkward to follow.
「〜にくい」 only means “takes effort”, not “can't”: 「この字は読みにくい」 can still be read; if you can't read it at all, say 「読めない」.

daily.title: Food that's hard to eat
daily.description: Explaining why something is awkward to eat.
daily.example: This fish has so many bones, it's hard to eat.

daily.title: Opening up to a friend
daily.description: Bringing up something you feel awkward saying.
daily.example: It's kind of hard to tell my parents, but...

daily.title: Choosing a product
daily.description: A clerk points out a product's strengths.
daily.example: This frying pan doesn't burn food easily.

work.title: Raising a difficult issue
work.description: Gently telling your boss something hard to say.
work.example: I'm sorry to have to say this, but it doesn't look like we'll make the deadline.

work.title: Giving feedback on a system
work.description: Telling the person in charge the system is clunky.
work.example: This system is a bit hard to use.

etymology: にくい is written 「憎い／難い」; the old word 「にくし」 originally meant "hateful, detestable". From "hateful to do" it extended to "hard to do", and as the second element of compound adjectives after the verb continuative form it expresses difficulty. Used on its own, 「憎い」 still keeps the meaning "hateful".
formation: 「〜にくい」 = verb masu-stem + 「にくい」 (「難い」: difficult); one theory says it shares a root with 「憎い」 (“hateful”). Together they form a new i-adjective meaning “this action takes effort”. With a person's intentional action → hard to do; with a change in a thing (「割れる」, 「燃える」) → unlikely to happen, which is often a plus (「割れにくいコップ」). With 「言う」, 「聞く」, or 「頼む」, the difficulty lies not in ability but in feelings, so it becomes “hard to bring up”.

similar.title: 〜づらい
similar.explanation: 「〜づらい」 (N3) focuses on physical or emotional discomfort in doing something (「足が痛くて歩きづらい」), mostly a person's subjective feeling; for properties of things you don't say ✕「割れづらい」 but 「割れにくい」.

similar.title: 〜がたい
similar.explanation: 「〜がたい」 (N3) means psychologically “hard to ..., almost impossible” (「信じがたい」, 「忘れがたい」); it's written and mostly attaches to verbs of thought and feeling. 「〜にくい」 is mostly about objective difficulty.

similar.title: 〜かねる
similar.explanation: 「〜かねる」 (N2) means “unable to (because of one's position)”, a formal, polite refusal (「お答えしかねます」); 「〜にくい」 only says something takes effort and isn't used to turn down clients.

meaning: The speaker's intention or plan: “I think I'll ...”, “I'm going to ...”. 「〜ようと思っている」 is a plan held for some time.
connection: Verb volitional form + と思う (行こう, 食べよう, しよう, 来よう)

senses.label: A decision now
senses.meaning: 「〜(よ)うと思う」 is a decision or idea made at the moment of speaking. The subject is first person: “I think I'll ...”.
senses.connection: Verb volitional form + と思う／と思います
examples: I think I'll go see a movie with friends this weekend.
I think I'll go to bed early tonight.

senses.label: A plan held for a while
senses.meaning: 「〜(よ)うと思っている」 is a plan you've had for some time. It can also be used for a third person.
senses.connection: Verb volitional form + と思っている／と思っています
examples: I'm planning to study abroad in Japan next year.
My brother has been thinking of buying a car.

senses.label: Meant to, but didn't
senses.meaning: 「〜(よ)うと思った」 often means you had the idea at the time but didn't end up doing it. Often followed by 「けど」 or 「のに」.
senses.connection: Verb volitional form + と思った(けど／が)
examples: I meant to call yesterday, but I forgot.
Just as I was about to go out, it started raining.

notes: It must be the volitional form, or the meaning changes completely: 「行くと思う」 = I think (he) will go (a guess); 「行こうと思う」 = I'm thinking of going.
「〜(よ)うと思う」 only describes your own plans; for others, use 「思っている」: ✕「兄は車を買おうと思う」→ ○「兄は車を買おうと思っている」.
The volitional form only works with volitional verbs: ✕「雨が降ろうと思う」 ✕「わかろうと思う」.

etymology: The volitional 〜(よ)う comes from the Classical Japanese conjectural auxiliary 「む」 (→ん→う), which expressed intention and conjecture; 「よう」 is the form 「う」 took after ichidan verbs. Classical 「〜むと思ふ」 already meant "I intend to ...", and modern 〜(よ)うと思う directly inherits this structure.
formation: 「〜(よ)うと思う」 = verb volitional form (「行こう」) + quoting particle 「と」 + 「思う」. The volitional form itself expresses the intention “(I) will do ...”; 「と」 quotes that intention as content, and 「思う」 says it's a thought in your mind → “thinking ‘let's go’” = I'm thinking of going. Because it quotes an intention in your own head, present-tense 「思う」 is only for the speaker; 「思っている」 becomes an ongoing state and can describe other people or plans held for some time. 「思った（けど）」 is “I thought so at the time”, often leading into “but I didn't”.

similar.title: 〜つもりだ
similar.explanation: 「〜つもりだ」 is a settled, firmer plan; 「〜(よ)うと思う」 is often an idea that just came up or a plan that may still change, with a softer tone.

similar.title: 〜予定だ
similar.explanation: 「〜予定だ」 is an objectively arranged schedule, not just your own wish (「来週出張する予定だ」); 「〜(よ)うと思う」 is only the speaker's intention.

similar.title: 〜ことにする
similar.explanation: 「〜ことにする」 (N3) means “decide (to do ...)”, stressing the moment of deciding (「留学することにした」); 「〜(よ)うと思う」 is just an idea or plan, not yet formally decided.

meaning: Shows what stage an action is at: about to start, in progress, or just finished. Also has related uses such as “almost ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form / ている-form / ta-form + ところだ

senses.label: About to
senses.meaning: The action is about to start but hasn't yet: “just about to ...”. Often with 「今から」, 「これから」, or 「ちょうど」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ところだ
examples: I'm just about to head out.
I'm about to have dinner.

senses.label: In the middle of
senses.meaning: The action is in progress: “in the middle of ...”. It stresses being in the process right now more than 「〜ている」 does.
senses.connection: Verb ている-form + ところだ (often with 「今」)
examples: I'm making dinner right now.
We're looking into that matter now.

senses.label: Just finished
senses.meaning: The action has just ended: “have just ...”. Often with 「たった今」, 「今」, or 「ちょうど」.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + ところだ
examples: I just got to the station.
I've just finished work.

senses.label: Almost
senses.meaning: 「〜ところだった」 means something almost happened but didn't. Often paired with 「もう少しで」 or 「危うく」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ところだった
examples: I almost missed the train.
That was close. I nearly hit a car.

senses.label: Just when ...
senses.meaning: 「〜ところに／へ」 means something else happened at that moment (someone came, the phone rang, etc.). 「〜ところを」 means you were seen or interrupted in the middle of something.
senses.connection: Verb (various forms) + ところに／ところへ／ところを
examples: Just as I was about to go out, the phone rang.
My teacher saw me while I was smoking.
Sorry to bother you when you're so busy.

notes: The verb form decides the meaning, so one mistake changes it: 「食べるところだ」 = about to eat; 「食べているところだ」 = in the middle of eating; 「食べたところだ」 = just finished eating.
「〜たところだ」 is only for the moment just past: ✕「先月日本に来たところです」→ ○「先月日本に来たばかりです」.
「お忙しいところ、すみません」 is a set business phrase when interrupting someone; jumping straight to the point without it can seem abrupt.
「〜ところだった」 means “nearly ... (but it didn't actually happen)”: 「遅れるところだった」 means you weren't late.

etymology: 「ところ」 is written 「所」, originally meaning "place, location". From a "position" in space it extended to a "position, stage" in the progress of time, giving the uses "about to / in the middle of / just finished". As a formal noun it is usually written in kana. (Compare English "at this point" used for time.)
formation: 「〜ところだ」 = verb + noun 「ところ」 (「所」: place) + 「だ」. 「ところ」 originally means a physical “place”; here it's used for time, meaning a “position” within the course of an action. The verb form decides where that position is: dictionary form = before the action, ている form = in the middle of it, た form = the point right after it ends. Because it refers to a single “point”, 「〜たところ」 can only mean “just now” and can't stretch back to last month; 「〜ところだった」 is “reached the point of ... (but didn't go past it)” → nearly.

similar.title: 〜たばかり
similar.explanation: 「〜たところ」 refers to the moment just after completion in physical time; 「〜たばかり」 is the speaker's psychological feeling that “not much time has passed”, usable even after several months (「先月来たばかりです」), and it can also modify nouns.

similar.title: 〜ところだった
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「〜ところだった」 (N3) is the past form of this pattern, used specifically for “nearly ...” (「もう少しで事故になるところだった」), which didn't actually happen.

similar.title: 〜ところに・〜ところへ
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「〜ところに・〜ところへ」 (N3) mean “just when ... (something else happened)” (「出かけるところへ電話が来た」), using the “point in time” as the setting for another event.

similar.title: 〜ところを
similar.explanation: Same origin. 「〜ところを」 (N3) means “at the moment when ... (be seen, be interrupted)” (「寝ているところを起こされた」); 「お忙しいところを」 is its set phrase use.

meaning: Not much time has passed since an action was completed: “just ...”. It stresses that the speaker feels the time was short.
connection: Verb ta-form + ばかりだ (casual: 〜たばっかり)

senses.label: Just did
senses.meaning: Not long has passed since the action. How long depends on the speaker's feeling; even a month later, you can still say “I just ...”.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + ばかりだ／ばかりです
examples: I just came to Japan last week.
I only just joined this company, so I don't know anything yet.

senses.label: Just ...ed (before a noun)
senses.meaning: 「〜たばかりの + noun」 describes a noun: “freshly ...ed”, “just ...ed”.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + ばかりの + noun
examples: I lost the umbrella I had just bought.
Newborn babies are really tiny.

senses.label: Only just ..., and yet
senses.meaning: 「〜たばかりなのに」 means “even though I only just ...”, with surprise or frustration.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + ばかりなのに
examples: I just ate, and I'm already hungry.
I just bought it, and it's already broken.

notes: The ta-form and te-form are one sound apart but mean completely different things: 「食べたばかりだ」 = just ate; 「食べてばかりいる」 = does nothing but eat.
A new employee saying 「入ったばかりなので、わかりません」 at work can sound like dodging responsibility; it's better to follow up with 「教えていただけますか」.
Don't use the casual 「〜たばっかり」 in formal situations or in writing.

etymology: 「ばかり」 comes from 「はかり」, the noun form of the verb 「計る（はかる）」 (to measure), originally meaning "estimate, approximate extent"; it later became voiced as the adverbial particle 「ばかり」, meaning "about, only, just". 〜たばかり thus means "only (that little time) since doing it", hence "have just done".
formation: 「〜たばかり」 = verb ta-form + adverbial particle 「ばかり」 + 「だ」. 「ばかり」 is generally thought to come from 「計る（はかる）」 (to measure), originally meaning “about, extent” and then “a narrow range”; after the ta-form (completed), it means “only a little time has passed since it was done” → just. Because “a little” is the speaker's subjective measure, it can be used even when months have objectively passed (「去年結婚したばかりだ」). 「ばかり」 is noun-like, so you can say 「〜たばかりの + noun」 to modify nouns, or 「〜たばかりなのに」.

similar.title: 〜ところだ
similar.explanation: 「〜たところだ」 refers to the instant just after something ended in physical time; 「〜たばかりだ」 is the psychological “not long ago”, can cover a longer span, and can modify nouns (「買ったばかりの本」).

similar.title: 〜たて
similar.explanation: 「〜たて」 (N3) means “freshly ...” (「焼きたてのパン」), attaches to only a few verbs, and stresses freshness; 「〜たばかり」 works with almost any verb.

similar.title: 〜てばかりいる
similar.explanation: Same origin, both using 「ばかり」. 「〜てばかりいる」 attaches to the te-form and means “always ..., do nothing but ...” (「遊んでばかりいる」); it has nothing to do with “just now”, so watch the difference in connection.
